newsitem.title: USA: Wash Mutual sees merger boosting EPS.
newsitem.headline: Wash Mutual sees merger boosting EPS.

text.p: Washington Mutual Savings Bank Chief Executive Kerry Killinger said in a telephone interview Thursday the proposed acquisition of Great Western Financial Corp will boost earnings five percent in 1998 and 11 percent in 1999.

Asked if Seattle-based Washington Mutual had the management depth to pull off the Great Western deal so soon after other deals such as the recent acquisition of American Savings, Killinger responded that the integration of American Savings had "proceeded in all respects ahead of schedule."
"We are growing households and new accounts at a rapid level," Killinger said, referring to American Savings. He said the integration of operating systems is in the final stages.
He also said the American Savings deal added to the senior executive and middle management ranks of Washington Mutual.

In the same telephone interview, Great Western President and Chief Executive John Maher said there was "no comparison" between Washington Mutual and Great Western's other suitor, H.F. Ahmanson and Co.
Washington Mutual is clearly "the superior company" based on its earnings history, asset quality and liquidity, he said.
"What we're talking about is creating a financial institution stretching from Seattle to San Diego, approaching $100 billion in assets and combining two very good companies," Maher said.

Ahmanson announced a stock bid for Great Western February 18. Great Western never formally rejected the offer but was widely believed to be looking for a "white knight" to save it from what was considered a hostile takeover. From the start, Washington Mutual was rumored to be the leading white knight candidate. Ahmanson, like Great Western, is based in Southern California.

Asked how Washington Mutual could achieve such targets as $340 million in annual pre-tax expense savings by 1999, Killinger said the company had been working with Great Western and had develped a "bottom-up plan" that included consolidation of about 100 branches and 100 lending offices.
"The biggest consolidations are in operating systems," he said, adding that Washington Mutual had invested millions of dollars in leading-edge technology.

Asked if his company were exceeding acquisition criteria it had used in the past, including such benchmarks as cost per household, Killinger said, "We're very comfortable with the (Great Western) purchase price that we have."
